words.definition: To display or make evident a feeling, quality, or trait through one's behavior.
words.example: Her steady voice evinced a calm that surprised everyone in the courtroom.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'convince' — when you evince a feeling, your behavior convinces others you truly have it.

words.definition: Having a firmly fixed habit that has lasted so long it seems impossible to change.
words.example: An inveterate gambler, he could not pass a casino without stopping to play.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'vetus' (old), the root of 'veteran' — an inveterate habit is a veteran habit.

words.definition: A thing placed in a period where it does not belong, especially something old surviving into the present.
words.example: A rotary telephone in a scene set in 2025 is a glaring anachronism.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'ana-' (against) + 'chronos' (time) — something set against its own time.

words.definition: Strongly opposed to political or social change and favoring a return to earlier conditions.
words.example: The reactionary faction wanted to repeal every reform passed in the last decade.
words.mnemonic: A 'reaction' against progress — recoiling backward toward the old ways.

words.definition: Moving backward or returning to an earlier and usually worse condition.
words.example: Cutting the research budget felt like a retrograde step for the whole country.
words.mnemonic: 'retro' (back) + 'grade' (step) — literally a backward step.

words.definition: A person who attacks or ridicules widely cherished beliefs, customs, or institutions.
words.example: As an iconoclast, she delighted in challenging the traditions everyone else took for granted.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'icon' (sacred image) + 'klastes' (breaker) — an image-breaker who smashes idols.

words.definition: A formal statement of the beliefs or principles that guide a person or group.
words.example: Honesty in every dealing was the creed by which the old merchant lived.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'credo' — 'I believe'; the same root behind 'credit' and 'credible'.

words.definition: Done or happening according to the usual practices of a group or place.
words.example: It was customary for the villagers to light lanterns on the first night of spring.
words.mnemonic: Think 'custom' — a customary act simply follows the customs everyone keeps.

words.definition: A set of actions performed regularly in the same way, often as a ceremony.
words.example: Her morning ritual began with black coffee and ten minutes of silence.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'rite' — a ritual is a rite you repeat.

words.definition: Firmly set up and accepted over a long time; well recognized and secure.
words.example: She left an established law firm to start her own risky venture.
words.mnemonic: 'Stable' hides inside — an established thing stands stable and settled.

words.definition: Favoring traditional values and cautious about making changes.
words.example: His conservative approach to investing meant he never chased risky stocks.
words.mnemonic: 'Conserve' — to conserve is to keep things exactly as they are.

words.definition: Involving or causing a complete and dramatic change in how things are done.
words.example: The smartphone was a revolutionary device that transformed daily life within a decade.
words.mnemonic: A 'revolution' turns everything around — revolutionary change spins the old order over.

words.definition: To reverse a decision or ruling, or to tip something so it falls.
words.example: The appeals court voted to overturn the lower court's verdict.
words.mnemonic: 'Over' + 'turn' — to turn something completely upside down.

words.definition: To update something with the latest methods, styles, or technology.
words.example: The factory spent millions to modernize its aging assembly lines.
words.mnemonic: 'Modern' + '-ize' — to make a thing modern.

words.definition: No longer useful, fashionable, or accepted because something better now exists.
words.example: Typewriters became outmoded once personal computers arrived in offices.
words.mnemonic: 'Out' of 'mode' (fashion) — simply out of style.

words.definition: No longer active, operating, or in existence.
words.example: We tried to redeem the coupon, but the company that issued it went defunct years ago.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'de-funked' — the funk (life, function) has been taken out of it.

words.definition: A tendency to remain unchanged or to do nothing.
words.example: The committee's inertia meant the same broken policy stayed in place for another decade.
words.mnemonic: From physics: an object at rest stays at rest — 'in-earth-ia,' stuck to the ground.

words.definition: To take the place of another, often through scheming or force.
words.example: The ambitious deputy quietly gathered allies until he could supplant the aging chairman.
words.mnemonic: Picture a weed's 'supple plant' shoving out the flower and rooting in its spot.

words.definition: To take the place of something older or less capable.
words.example: The new safety regulations supersede the guidelines your team was trained on last year.
words.mnemonic: 'Super' + 'sede' (to sit) — a superior thing sits down in the old one's chair.

words.definition: To formally end a law, system, or practice.
words.example: Reformers spent decades campaigning to abolish the tax that crushed small farmers.
words.mnemonic: 'A-bol-ish' — take a bowling ball and knock the whole system down for good.

words.definition: To take apart or break down into separate pieces.
words.example: Engineers had to dismantle the entire engine just to reach the cracked valve inside.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis' (undo) + 'mantle' — strip off the cloak/covering piece by piece.

words.definition: To destroy or wipe out something completely.
words.example: The vaccination campaign aimed to eradicate the disease so no child would ever catch it again.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'radix' = root; think of yanking a weed out by its roots so nothing regrows.

words.definition: To secretly undermine the power or authority of something.
words.example: Leaking the memos was his quiet way to subvert a leadership he could not openly challenge.
words.mnemonic: 'Sub' (under) + 'vert' (turn) — turn something over from underneath, toppling it.

words.definition: To attack or call into question as false or dishonest.
words.example: The lawyer tried to impugn the witness, hinting she had lied about everything she saw.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'pug' — imagine a pugnacious boxer throwing punches at someone's honesty.

words.definition: To make something seem less important than it really is.
words.example: The manager tried to downplay the data breach, calling it a minor technical hiccup.
words.mnemonic: Literally turn the volume 'down' when you 'play' the news, so it sounds small.

words.definition: Regarded as too important or holy to be changed or criticized.
words.example: In her house, Sunday dinner was sacrosanct — no work call could ever interrupt it.
words.mnemonic: 'Sacro' (sacred) + 'sanct' (holy) — doubly holy, like an untouchable altar.

words.definition: Unwilling to change because of tradition or narrow opinions.
words.example: The hidebound faculty rejected online classes, insisting chalkboards had worked for a century.
words.mnemonic: 'Hide' + 'bound' — wrapped so tightly in old leather (hide) it can't move or bend.

words.definition: Having a narrow outlook limited to a small local area.
words.example: His parochial views crumbled the moment he left the village and traveled abroad.
words.mnemonic: From 'parish' — thinking no bigger than your tiny local church district.

words.definition: To officially cancel or revoke a law, order, or agreement.
words.example: After the backlash, the board voted to rescind the fee it had approved that morning.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-scissored' — take scissors and cut the signed decree back out.

words.definition: Saying the same thing twice using different words, adding no new information.
words.example: "It's a free gift you get for nothing" is a tautology that made the editor wince.
words.mnemonic: "TAUT-ology" — a rope pulled TAUT and then pulled TAUT again: the same tension stated twice.

words.definition: The quality of seeming real or true to life.
words.example: The novelist visited coal mines for a week so her story would have the verisimilitude critics praised.
words.mnemonic: Latin roots: "veri" (truth, as in verify) + "simil" (similar) — similar to the truth.

words.definition: Strikingly suitable and relevant to the matter at hand.
words.example: During the debate on privacy, she cited an apposite court ruling that silenced her opponent.
words.mnemonic: Think "a-POSIT" — a point positioned exactly where it fits, right on the spot.

words.definition: A rule or order issued by a city or town government.
words.example: A local ordinance forbids leaf-blowers before eight in the morning.
words.mnemonic: It has 'order' inside it — a local order to obey. (Don't confuse it with 'ordnance,' meaning weapons.)

words.definition: Laws that have been formally enacted, or the process of creating them.
words.example: Congress debated the healthcare legislation for months before finally holding a vote.
words.mnemonic: 'Legis' is Latin for law (as in 'legal') plus '-lation' — the making of laws.

words.definition: An official rule that controls how something is done.
words.example: Safety regulations require every worker on the site to wear a hardhat.
words.mnemonic: Think 'regular' — it keeps things regular, orderly, and within limits.

words.definition: To officially forbid something by law or rule.
words.example: The posted sign clearly prohibits swimming whenever no lifeguard is on duty.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'pro-HIB-it' — picture a giant PROhibition sign slamming down: NO.

words.definition: To officially condemn or denounce something and forbid it as dangerous.
words.example: The regime proscribed the opposition party, so joining it became a crime overnight.
words.mnemonic: 'Pro-SCRIBE' — officials scribe your name onto a banned list. (Opposite of 'prescribe,' which recommends.)

words.definition: To hold back or restrain a feeling, action, or group by force.
words.example: She fought to repress a laugh during the solemn funeral service.
words.mnemonic: 'RE-press' — you press it back down again, like shoving a jack-in-the-box lid shut.

words.definition: To treat a group harshly and unfairly through prolonged use of power.
words.example: For decades the dictator oppressed anyone who dared to speak freely in public.
words.mnemonic: 'OP-press' — those on top press down on the weak below them.

words.definition: To force a people or group into obedience and submission.
words.example: The empire sent armies to subjugate every tribe living along the river.
words.mnemonic: 'SUB-JUG-ate' — put them 'sub' (under) a 'jug'/yoke, like oxen forced to plow.

words.definition: Cruel, unjust, and absolute use of power by a ruler.
words.example: The revolution promised to end centuries of tyranny under a ruthless crown.
words.mnemonic: It contains 'tyrant' — the harsh, all-controlling ruler whose rule this describes.

words.definition: A system in which one ruler holds total power and wields it harshly.
words.example: Under his despotism, no court could ever overturn a single royal decree.
words.mnemonic: 'Despot' sounds like 'the spot' — the ruler who owns every spot and answers to no one.

words.definition: Demanding strict obedience and allowing people little personal freedom.
words.example: The authoritarian principal banned any student club she had not personally approved.
words.mnemonic: Built on 'authority' — this person worships authority and expects total compliance.

words.definition: Ruling alone with unlimited power and no need for anyone's consent.
words.example: The CEO's autocratic style meant major decisions were made without asking anyone.
words.mnemonic: 'Auto' (self) + 'cratic' (rule) — self-rule, where one person decides everything.

words.definition: Government or control held by a small, privileged group of people.
words.example: A handful of wealthy families ran the entire country as a tight oligarchy.
words.mnemonic: 'Oligo' (few, in Greek) + 'archy' (rule) — rule by the few.
